name: De La Riva Sweeps
keyCorrections: If they strip your hook, your angle was wrong — re-insert the hook from a sharper angle.
If you can't off-balance them, your sleeve grip is too far from your hip — pull it closer.
If they step back and avoid the sweep, extend your hook and transition to a heel hook or leg entanglement entry.
description: Use the inside De La Riva hook and sleeve grip to off-balance the passer, enter X-guard or single-leg X, or sweep directly to top position.
shortInstruction: Inside hook, sleeve grip, angle off the hip — DLR is the gateway to the entire open guard system.
summary: De La Riva (DLR) guard is the most common open guard in modern no-gi. The inside hook on the opponent's near leg, combined with a sleeve or ankle grip, gives you control over their base. By pulling their sleeve across your body and simultaneously hooking their leg, you create an angle that off-balances them forward and to one side. This opens entries into X-guard, single-leg X, or direct sweeps.
whyItWorks: The DLR hook on the inside of their leg blocks their forward pass while giving you a lever to off-balance.
The sleeve grip connected to your far hip creates a diagonal tension that breaks their base.
DLR entries lead to the strongest sweeping positions in no-gi: X-guard and single-leg X.
Danaher principle: DLR removes one of their passing legs, reducing their passing options by 50%.
It works excellently against a standing passer — when they stand to pass, DLR is your counter.
commonMistakes: Letting the DLR hook get shallow or stripped — a deep hook is essential for control.
Holding the sleeve grip at your hip instead of pulling it across your body — the cross-body tension creates the off-balance.
Fighting for DLR when the passer is already on their knees — DLR is for standing passers.
Staying flat on your back — DLR requires you to be on your side to generate power.
coachingCues: Deep hook, cross-body sleeve, on your side.
Pull the sleeve, hook the leg — the angle creates the sweep.
DLR to X-guard is one movement, not two.
If they're on their knees, DLR is the wrong guard — switch to half guard or knee shield.
safetySummary: Do not let them grab your DLR hook foot and twist — protect your knee by keeping the hook active and mobile.
When off-balancing, keep your head off the mat to prevent guillotine entries.
If they step over your DLR hook, immediately switch to reverse DLR or recover guard.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: DLR hook + sleeve grip → off-balance them forward → opponent posts → enter X-guard or SLX → sweep or attack legs.

decisionTree.action: If they step forward (over the hook), go to deep DLR or waiter sweep.
If they step back, extend into X-guard and sweep forward.
DLR is the entry; X-guard and SLX are the destination.

moneyDetails: Your DLR hook must be deep — the ball of your foot hooks inside their thigh, not their calf.
Pull their sleeve to your far hip, not straight down — diagonal tension breaks their base more effectively.
Stay on your side, not your back — being on your side gives your hook more range and power.
When they resist the off-balance by stepping back, that's your X-guard entry — extend the hook and slide your other leg to their hip.
nextStep: After DLR sweeps, learn X-guard and single-leg X transitions to complete the open guard system.
fixItFast: Hook keeps slipping? Dig it deeper — foot should hook inside the thigh, not behind the knee.
Can't off-balance? Pull the sleeve across your body, not toward you — cross-body tension is key.
They keep passing? Your DLR hook is too shallow or you're too flat on your back — sit up to your side.
